title: The writers of Scripture read it figuratively
source_text: Εἰ δ᾿ ἀδεκάστως ἀνεγνώκει τὴν γραφὴν ὁ Κέλσος, οὐκ ἂν εἶπεν οὐχ οἷα ἀλληγορίαν ἐπιδέχεσθαι εἶναι τὰ γράμματα ἡμῶν, ἀπὸ γὰρ τῶν προφητειῶν, ἐν αἷς τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς ἱστορίας γέγραπται, οὐχ ὡς ἀπὸ τῆς ἱστορίας ἔστι προσαχθῆναι καὶ ταῖς ἱστορίαις ὡς σκοπῷ τροπολογίας γεγραμμέναις καὶ σοφώτατα οἰκονομηθείσαις, ἐστοχασμένως τοῦ τε πλήθους τῶν ἁπλούστερον πιστευόντων καὶ τῶν ὀλίγων μετὰ συνέσεως ἐξετάζειν τὰ πράγματα βουλομένων ἢ καὶ δυναμένων, καὶ εἰ μὲν οἱ σήμερον νομιζόμενοι κατὰ Κέλσον ἐπιεικεῖς ἀπὸ Ἰουδαίων καὶ Χριστιανῶν ἠλληγόρουν τὰ γεγραμμένα, τάχα ἂν πιθανόν τι λέγειν ὑπενοεῖτο ὁ Κέλσος· ἐπεὶ δ᾿ αὐτοὶ οἱ πατέρες τῶν δογμάτων καὶ συγγραφεῖς τὰ τοιαῦτα τροπολογοῦσι, τί ἐστιν ἄλλο ὑπονοῆσαι ἢ ὅτι οὕτως ἐγράφη, ὥστε τροπολογεῖσθαι αὐτὰ κατὰ τὸν προηγούμενον νοῦν; ὀλίγα δ᾿ ἀπὸ πάνυ πολλῶν παραθησόμεθα πρὸς τὸ δεῖξαι ὅτι μάτην συκοφαντεῖ τοὺς λόγους ὁ Κέλσος ὡς οὐχ οἵους τε ἐπιδέξασθαι ἀλληγορίαν, φησὶ δὴ ὁ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἀπόστολος Παῦλος· „ἐν τῷ νόμῳ γέγραπται· οὐ φιμώσεις βοῦν ἀλοῶντα, μὴ τῶν βοῶν μέλει τῷ θεῷ; ἢ δι᾿ ἡμᾶς πάντως λέγει; δι᾿ ἡμᾶς γὰρ ἐγράφη ὅτι ὀφείλει ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι ὁ ἀροτριῶν ἀροτριᾶν, καὶ ὁ ἀλοῶν ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι τοῦ μετέχειν,“ καὶ ἀλλαχοῦ φησιν ὁ αὐτός· „γέγραπται γὰρ ὅτι ἕνεκεν τούτου καταλείψει ἄνθρωπος τὸν πατέρα καὶ τὴν μητέρα καὶ προσκολληθήσεται πρὸς τὴν γυναῖκα αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν, τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστὶν, ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω εἰς Χριστὸν καὶ εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν“· καὶ πάλιν ἐν ἄλλῳ τόπῳ· „οἴδαμεν δ᾿ ὅτι οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν πάντες ὑπὸ τὴν νεφέλην ἦσαν, καὶ πάντες διὰ τῆς θαλάσσης διῆλθον, καὶ πάντες εἰς τὸν Μωϋσῆς ἐβαπτίσαντο ἐν τῇ νεφέλῃ καὶ ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ.“ εἶθ᾿ ἑρμηνεύων τὴν περὶ τοῦ μάννα ἱστορίαν καὶ τὴν περὶ τοῦ ὕδατος ἐκ πέτρας ἐξεληλυθέναι ἀναγεγραμμένου παραδόξως τοιαῦτα λέγει· „καὶ πάντες τὸ αὐτὸ βρῶμα πνευματικὸν ἔφαγον, καὶ πάντες τὸ αὐτὸ πνευματικὸν ἔπιον πόμα· ἔπινον γὰρ ἐκ πνευματικῆς ἀκολουθούσης πέτρας, ἡ δὲ πέτρα ἦν ὁ Χριστός,“ παριστὰς δὲ ὁ Ἀσὰφ ὅτι „προβλήματα“ καὶ „παραβολαί“ εἰσιν αἱ κατὰ τὴν Ἔξοδον ἱστορίαι καὶ τοὺς Ἀριθμοὺς, ὡς ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ τῶν Ψαλμῶν γέγραπται, μέλλων αὐτῶν ὑπομιμνήσκεσθαι τοῦτον προοιμιάζεται τὸν τρόπον· „προσέχετε λαός μου τῷ νόμῳ μου, κλίνατε τὸ οὖς ὑμῶν εἰς τὰ ῥήματα τοῦ στόματός μου, ἀνοίξω ἐν παραβολαῖς τὸ στόμα μου, φθέγξομαι προβλήματα ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς, ὅσα ἠκούσαμεν καὶ ἔγνωμεν αὐτὰ. καὶ οἱ πατέρες ἡμῶν διηγήσαντο ἡμῖν.“
pass_a_gloss: If Celsus had read (ἀναγινώσκω) the Scripture without bias (ἀδεκάστως), he would not have said that our writings (γράμματα) are not such as to admit (ἐπιδέχομαι) allegory. For from the prophecies (προφητεία), in which things from history (ἱστορία) are written not as from history, one may be brought (προσάγω) also to the histories as written with the aim (σκοπός) of figurative sense (τροπολογία) and most wisely arranged (οἰκονομέω), aiming at (στοχάζομαι) both the multitude (πλῆθος) of those believing more simply (ἁπλούστερον) and the few wishing or able to examine (ἐξετάζω) matters with understanding (σύνεσις). And if those now thought reasonable (ἐπιεικής) according to Celsus among Jews and Christians allegorized the writings, perhaps Celsus would be supposed to say something plausible (πιθανός); but since the very fathers (πατέρες) of the doctrines (δόγμα) and writers (συγγραφεύς) interpret such things figuratively (τροπολογέω), what else is to be supposed than that they were written so as to be figuratively interpreted according to the leading (προηγούμενος) sense (νοῦς)? We shall set beside (παρατίθημι) a few out of very many to show that Celsus vainly slanders (συκοφαντέω) the words as unable to admit allegory. Paul, the apostle of Jesus, says: 'in the law it is written: you shall not muzzle (φιμόω) an ox threshing (ἀλοάω); is it for oxen God cares (μέλει)? or does he say it altogether (πάντως) for us? for us it was written, that the plougher (ἀροτριάω) ought to plough in hope, and the thresher in hope of partaking (μετέχω)'; elsewhere: 'for it is written: for this a man will leave father and mother and be joined (προσκολλάω) to his wife, and the two will be into one flesh; this mystery (μυστήριον) is great, but I speak toward Christ and toward the church (ἐκκλησία)'; again: 'we know that our fathers were all under the cloud (νεφέλη), and all went through the sea, and all were baptized (βαπτίζω) into Moses in the cloud and the sea.' Then interpreting (ἑρμηνεύω) the story of the manna and of the water recorded to have come out of a rock marvellously (παραδόξως) he says: 'and all ate the same spiritual (πνευματικός) food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from a spiritual following (ἀκολουθέω) rock, and the rock was Christ.' Asaph, presenting that the histories in Exodus and Numbers are 'problems' (πρόβλημα, riddles) and 'parables' (παραβολή), as written in the book of Psalms, about to recall them, makes this prelude (προοιμιάζομαι): 'attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth; I will open my mouth in parables, I will utter (φθέγγομαι) problems from the beginning, what we heard and knew, and our fathers recounted (διηγέομαι) to us.'
pass_b_english: If Celsus had read the Scripture without prejudice, he would not have said that our writings “are not such as to admit allegory.” For from the prophecies, in which events drawn from history are written, but not as history, one may be led to see that the histories too were written with a figurative meaning as their aim, and were arranged with the greatest wisdom, with regard both for the multitude of those who believe more simply and for the few who wish, or are even able, to examine matters with understanding. And if it were those among Jews and Christians today whom Celsus counts reasonable who allegorized what is written, Celsus might perhaps be thought to be saying something plausible. But since the fathers and writers of the doctrines themselves interpret such things figuratively, what else is one to suppose than that they were written so as to be read figuratively in their primary sense?

We shall set out a few passages out of very many, to show that Celsus slanders the Scriptures in vain as incapable of admitting allegory. Paul, the apostle of Jesus, says: “It is written in the law, ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain’ (Deuteronomy 25:4). Is it for oxen that God cares? Or does he speak entirely for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the one who ploughs ought to plough in hope, and the one who threshes ought to thresh in hope of a share” (1 Corinthians 9:9–10). And elsewhere the same apostle says: “For it is written, ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh’ (Genesis 2:24). This mystery is great; but I speak with reference to Christ and to the church” (Ephesians 5:31–32). And again in another place: “We know that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:1–2).

Then, interpreting the story of the manna (Exodus 16:14–15) and the account of the water that is recorded to have come miraculously out of a rock (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11), he says this: “And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:3–4). And Asaph, showing that the histories in Exodus and Numbers are “riddles” and “parables,” as is written in the book of Psalms, begins in this way when he is about to recall them: “Pay attention, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter riddles from of old, such things as we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:1–3).

κατὰ τὸν προηγούμενον νοῦν: 'read figuratively in their primary sense'
ἢ καί: 'wish, or are even able'
Genesis 2:24 as Origen quotes it: 'leave father and mother' (no 'his')
παραδόξως ... ἀναγεγραμμένου: 'recorded to have come miraculously out of a rock'
Deuteronomy 25:4, 1 Corinthians 9:9–10, Genesis 2:24, Ephesians 5:31–32, 1 Corinthians 10:1–4, Psalm 77:1–3 LXX = 78:1–3 checked

The second sentence is compressed and its syntax uncertain: I take οὐχ ὡς ἀπὸ τῆς ἱστορίας with γέγραπται ('written, but not as history') and ταῖς ἱστορίαις as the goal of προσαχθῆναι ('led to the histories, as written with a figurative aim'). 'The very fathers and writers of the doctrines' are the biblical authors (Paul, Asaph), against Celsus's 'reasonable' moderns. 1 Corinthians 10:1: Origen's text has οἴδαμεν δ᾿ ὅτι ('we know that') where the NT reads 'I do not want you to be ignorant that'; translated as Origen quotes it. The source has εἰς τὸν Μωϋσῆς (sic, read Μωϋσῆν). Ephesians 5:31 is introduced in Origen's text by γέγραπται γὰρ ὅτι, which is not in the NT wording; kept. Origen's Genesis 2:24 wording has τὸν πατέρα καὶ τὴν μητέρα without αὐτοῦ, so 'father and mother' without 'his'. 1 Corinthians 9:10 ἀλοῶν ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι τοῦ μετέχειν: the verb 'thresh' is supplied by English idiom from the parallel clause. 'A spiritual rock that followed them': 'them' is supplied for English; the Greek participle has no object. Psalm 77:1–3 LXX = Psalm 78:1–3 English; πρόβλημα rendered 'riddles'; ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς 'from of old'. The manna and rock-water allusions are cited to Exodus 16 and Exodus 17:6 / Numbers 20:11.
